bme-y12-u3-global-brands-and-market-feas.title: The value of a global brand

blocks.text: A global brand uses a recognisable identity across international markets. Familiarity can reduce perceived purchase risk, support consistent positioning and make coordinated advertising more efficient. Brand equity can help a business introduce related products and negotiate distribution.

A global reputation also links markets: a quality failure or misleading claim in one country can damage trust elsewhere. Brand recognition does not remove the need for local relevance, reliable service and legal compliance.

Estimate the size and characteristics of the target segment, likely purchase frequency, willingness to pay and competing uses of income. Consumption patterns can vary by climate, culture, household needs and how the product is used.

Use relevant research rather than population size alone. A large population may contain only a small segment able and willing to buy a premium product. Combine secondary data with customer testing, distributor insight and realistic assumptions.

Identify direct and indirect competitors, their prices, product features, distribution, reputation and likely response. A market gap is useful only if customers value the proposed difference enough to support profitable sales.

A premium bicycle brand might face strong local repair networks rather than simply rival bicycle prices. It could need service partners to compete effectively. Compare the firm’s strengths with what customers actually require in that market.

Assess market demand alongside capacity, entry cost, logistics, finance, legal requirements and risk. Model conservative and optimistic outcomes to see which assumptions have the greatest influence on viability.

A recommendation should state why entry is feasible, which strategy fits the evidence and what would trigger a review. If the evidence is weak, recommend a controlled pilot or further research rather than presenting an unsupported forecast as fact.

Standardisation keeps important marketing elements consistent across countries. It can reduce design and production costs and reinforce a coherent identity. Adaptation changes elements to suit local needs, language, regulation or competition.

Businesses often combine both approaches. A consistent visual identity can coexist with locally suitable packaging and messages. The decision depends on whether savings from consistency outweigh the benefits and costs of responding to differences.

rows: Pronunciation, unintended meaning or trademark availability
Climate, safety, sizes, tastes or technical standards
Different competitors, incomes or customer priorities

blocks.text: Adaptation should be based on research and testing. A literal translation can preserve words while losing the intended meaning.

Positioning is the place a business wants its brand to occupy in the target customer’s mind relative to competitors. A brand seen as everyday value in one country may be a premium imported product in another because of price, scarcity or associations.

Illustrative example: a cereal producer keeps its name and design but changes portion size, flavour and package language. It tests the offer with the intended segment and compares additional adaptation costs with expected contribution and brand effects.
Choose which elements to keep and which to change, explaining each decision through market evidence. Consider consistency, customer understanding, production complexity and regulatory requirements.

Measure awareness, perceived value, conversion and repeat purchase after entry. A campaign with high recognition but poor repeat sales may indicate product or service problems. Review the entire offer instead of assuming a new advertisement will solve every issue.

A strategic alliance brings businesses together to pursue shared objectives while the precise ownership and contractual arrangements vary. Global growth strategies can provide access to technology, distribution, local knowledge, capacity or finance.

Compare control, integration cost, cultural fit and dependence on partners. The syllabus groups several growth arrangements together, but a merger or acquisition changes ownership more fundamentally than a typical contractual alliance.

Outsourcing contracts a task or function to an external provider. A global provider may offer specialist expertise, scale or access to a location. It can allow the business to focus on its own strengths.

The firm may lose direct control, become dependent on the supplier or face quality and labour-standard risks. Specify service expectations, monitoring, contingency plans and responsibilities. Lower quoted cost is insufficient if failure costs or ethical risks are high.

A merger combines businesses into one organisation. An acquisition occurs when one business purchases control of another. Both can provide rapid access to markets, assets, skills and established customers.

Purchase and integration costs, incompatible systems and organisational cultures can undermine expected benefits. Competition and other regulatory requirements may apply. A proposal needs evidence that benefits exceed integration costs and that people and systems can work together.

A joint venture involves parties contributing resources to an agreed undertaking, often through a jointly owned entity. A local partner may contribute market knowledge and relationships while another partner provides technology or capital.

Shared control can reduce the resources each party commits but also create disagreement over objectives, profits and decisions. Agreements should clarify contributions, responsibilities, intellectual property, dispute processes and exit arrangements.

Franchising allows a franchisee to operate using a franchisor’s brand and business system under an agreement, usually for fees. International franchising can expand a brand using local investment and management.

The franchisor needs training and monitoring to protect quality and reputation. Franchisees face fees and limits on independence. Local adaptation, supply arrangements and legal requirements must be considered. Poor performance by one operator can affect the wider brand.

Illustrative case: a small Australian service business wants overseas customers but lacks local knowledge. A joint venture could share risk and combine expertise, while franchising could expand using local operators if the system is proven and transferable.

Compare the options against the business’s objective and resources. Explain the main trade-off, such as shared control or monitoring cost, and recommend safeguards. The fastest expansion route may not provide the best long-term fit.

Exporters can face currency fluctuations and non-payment of monies. Currency risk concerns changes in the domestic value of foreign-currency receipts or costs. Non-payment risk concerns the customer failing to meet agreed payment obligations.

These risks can occur separately. A customer may pay in full while an adverse exchange-rate movement reduces the exporter’s Australian-dollar return. Conversely, a favourable exchange rate offers little benefit if the customer never pays.

bme-y12-u3-financial-risk-in-export-mark.title: Currency movements and the invoice currency

blocks.text: An Australian-dollar appreciation means one Australian dollar buys more foreign currency. A depreciation means it buys less. When an exporter has an unhedged fixed foreign-currency receivable, appreciation generally reduces the Australian dollars received on conversion.

If the sale is invoiced in Australian dollars, the immediate conversion exposure may fall on the customer, but the exporter can still face competitiveness effects. Timing, foreign-currency costs and hedging alter the final effect. Always state the currency and assumptions.

Assume an unhedged US-dollar invoice, immediate conversion at each quoted rate and no fees. Appreciation from US$0.65 to US$0.70 per Australian dollar reduces the receipt by $1,098.90. These are teaching rates, not current quotations.

A customer may fail to pay because of insolvency, a dispute about quality or delivery, deliberate default or restrictions on transferring money. Delayed payment also creates a working-capital problem, even when payment eventually arrives.

The exporter may have already paid wages, suppliers and freight. Assess buyer creditworthiness, country risk and contract terms before accepting an order. Large sales to one buyer increase concentration risk. Clear documentation helps but cannot remove every cause of default.

Illustrative case: a new overseas customer requests 90-day credit in its own currency. The exporter faces both a long foreign-currency exposure and uncertainty about payment. It should assess the customer, cash-flow needs and available protection.

A reasoned response links each identified risk to a suitable control. A forward contract can manage a known currency exposure but does not guarantee that the customer will pay. Credit insurance addresses specified non-payment risks but does not automatically fix an exchange rate.

Accurate contracts, invoices, shipping documents and payment instructions establish what has been agreed. Specify product requirements, price, invoice currency, due date, delivery arrangements and dispute procedures. Consistent documentation supports customs clearance and payment processing.

Documents reduce ambiguity and support enforcement, but they do not guarantee that a buyer is solvent or willing to pay. Errors or mismatched details can delay payment, especially where a bank examines documents under a letter of credit.

Advance payment requires the buyer to pay before the exporter ships or supplies. Once cleared funds are received, exposure to that buyer’s non-payment for the prepaid amount is greatly reduced. The importer instead faces the risk of non-delivery or unsatisfactory goods.

Demanding full prepayment can make an offer less competitive. Deposits and staged payments may share risk. Prepayment does not automatically remove every currency risk: a business can remain exposed before conversion or on foreign-currency costs.

A documentary letter of credit is a bank undertaking to pay when the required complying documents are presented under its terms. It can reduce reliance on the buyer’s willingness to pay, particularly in a new trading relationship.

The exporter must check the issuing bank, country risk, expiry dates and documentary requirements. Banks deal with documents rather than physically guaranteeing the quality of goods. Fees, discrepancies and timing matter. A confirmed letter of credit may add an undertaking from a second bank.

Under documentary collection, banks handle documents and collection instructions. With documents against payment, the buyer generally receives the relevant documents after paying. This offers more documentary control than open-account trading.

The collecting bank does not ordinarily guarantee payment. A buyer may refuse the documents, leaving goods stranded and creating storage or return costs. Compare this arrangement with a letter of credit rather than treating them as equivalent guarantees.

Trade credit or export credit insurance can cover specified losses from buyer non-payment, subject to policy terms. Some cover may include specified political risks. Transit or shipping insurance addresses covered loss or damage to goods during transport.

Check premiums, exclusions, excesses, credit limits, claim conditions and waiting periods. A policy may reimburse only part of a loss and may not provide cash immediately. Match the insurance to the actual exposure; cargo cover does not automatically cover an unpaid invoice.

A foreign exchange forward contract agrees an exchange rate today for a specified currency amount to be exchanged on a future date. It is generally arranged with a financial provider, separately from the sales contract. It provides greater certainty over the Australian-dollar value of a known exposure.

The business is committed under the contract and may forgo favourable currency movements. If the customer pays late or cancels, the exporter may still have an obligation to the provider. Amounts and timing should therefore match expected receipts as closely as practicable.

A currency option gives its holder the right, without an obligation, to exchange currency at an agreed rate within the specified terms. It can offer protection against an adverse movement while allowing the holder to benefit from a favourable market rate.

The flexibility generally requires a premium. Compare the premium and other costs with the value of flexibility and the certainty of a forward. An option is not a guarantee of higher profit and does not remove buyer default risk.

Illustrative case: a first-time customer places a large US-dollar order. The exporter could seek a deposit, use a suitable letter of credit, consider credit insurance and hedge the remaining expected currency receipt. Clear documents support every stage.

Evaluate cost, customer acceptance, cash flow and residual risk. Controls should work together: hedging an amount unlikely to be received can create a new problem. Review exposures as delivery dates and customer circumstances change.
